column2:
Short answer
ST05 helps inspect traced database access for a scoped execution. SAT shows ABAP runtime distribution and call behavior. SQL Monitor helps find important SQL across a broader workload. A database execution plan explains how the database processes a statement. I select the tool according to whether the bottleneck is database work, ABAP processing, or call volume.

Example
For a slow report, identify the expensive processing segment, trace a representative run, and compare executions, rows, and time. In cloud editions the available tools and permissions differ; use the supported ADT or monitoring equivalent for that environment.

Avoid
The slowest individual SQL statement may not be the largest total cost if another cheap statement is executed thousands of times.

column1: SQL-11 | Does SAP HANA remove the need for indexes and performance tuning?
column2:
Short answer
No. HANA's column storage, compression, and execution engine change the tradeoffs, but large scans, poor selectivity, row multiplication, and expensive intermediate results still matter. Secondary indexes can help specific access patterns and also consume memory and maintenance effort. I evaluate the actual table organization, workload, and execution evidence before proposing an index.

Example
A selective lookup repeatedly filtering the same attribute combination may benefit from a supported secondary index. That is different from assuming a SQL Server-style clustered index controls physical row ordering. HANA column-store index structures have their own documented behavior.

Avoid
Do not say HANA needs no indexes or that every primary key is a clustered index with a predictable physical row order.

column1: SQL-12 | When is table buffering appropriate?
column2:
Short answer
Buffering can benefit small, relatively stable data read frequently through access patterns supported by the ABAP table buffer. It is usually unsuitable for highly volatile transactional data or requirements needing immediate cross-instance freshness. I check the table's buffering configuration and statement behavior, because some query forms bypass the buffer and buffering changes consistency tradeoffs.

Example
A small customizing table may be a candidate after checking change frequency and access. An order status updated continuously is different. The ABAP table buffer is separate from HANA caches and internal tables held by an individual application session.

Avoid
Buffering is not universally faster, and reading buffered data does not guarantee immediate visibility of every change across application servers.

column1: SQL-13 | What are normalization and denormalization, and how do they affect ABAP design?
column2:
Short answer
Normalization organizes relational data around dependencies to reduce update, insert, and delete anomalies. First normal form avoids repeating groups; second removes partial dependency on a candidate key; third addresses unsuitable transitive dependencies of non-key attributes. Denormalization deliberately duplicates or precomputes data for a measured need and requires an explicit consistency strategy.

Example
Keeping a customer's current address on every order row creates update problems if those copies are intended to remain synchronized. An immutable address snapshot on a historical invoice can instead be a deliberate business requirement. Clarify the semantics before calling duplication a defect.

Avoid
NoSQL is not automatically faster or better for large data, and normalization is not a rule against all intentionally stored business snapshots.

column1: SQL-14 | When is AMDP justified, and what risks must you address?
column2:
Short answer
I consider AMDP when supported ABAP SQL or CDS cannot express a necessary database-specific operation well, or measurement shows that keeping a substantial calculation on HANA avoids repeated large transfers. I account for SQLScript skills, testability, dependencies, client and authorization handling, and the release's restrictions. Database pushdown must preserve business correctness, not just reduce ABAP code.

Example
A complex analytical calculation may justify an AMDP or CDS table function after simpler options are evaluated. A plain filtered SELECT normally does not. Database logic must not assume that selecting underlying tables automatically enforces the DCL of a CDS entity.

Avoid
AMDP is not a universal performance upgrade, and an AMDP method should not introduce an independent commit into an application transaction.

column1: ODATA-01 | When would you choose OData V4 rather than V2?
column2:
Short answer
Prefer V4 for new supported transactional RAP services, while checking the actual Fiori elements or integration consumer and backend release. Keep V2 where required by an existing contract or consumer. V4 has first-class actions and functions and different protocol details; it is not simply a faster V2 switch.

Example
Draft, determinations and validations are RAP capabilities rather than exclusive V4 features. Verify draft and non-draft support for the specific UI template and SAPUI5 version.

Avoid
Neither RAP nor draft automatically implies that V2 is impossible; Gateway is not exclusively V2.

column1: ODATA-02 | What does $metadata describe?
column2:
Short answer
It describes the service contract: entity types, properties, keys, relationships, operations and relevant annotations. Clients use it to understand types and available operations. Metadata is separate from instance data, and the actual endpoint must be checked after model or binding changes.

Example
A missing action button may result from an unexposed projection action, missing metadata or UI support. Inspect the contract before debugging the handler implementation.

Avoid
A database field is not automatically visible in the service just because it exists in persistence.

column2:
Short answer

Example
Request a small field set, a selective filter and a stable key-based order. Use free-text $search only where the service exposes and implements that capability.

column1: ODATA-04 | How do paging and total count work in V2 and V4?
column2:
Short answer
Apply filtering before count and paging, and ensure a stable order. V2 commonly uses $inlinecount=allpages, while V4 uses $count=true for an inline total; the /$count resource returns a count. Server-driven paging can return a next link that clients should follow.

Example
A total of 500 with a page of 20 is valid. Returning 20 as the total because only 20 rows were fetched breaks page navigation. Concurrent changes may still affect offset-based paging.

Avoid
Do not invent one generic SET_COUNT method for every Gateway implementation; use the actual response contract.

column1: ODATA-05 | What is the difference between actions and functions?
column2:
Short answer
In V4 a function is side-effect-free in the protocol sense and is used for retrieval or calculation. An action may have side effects and is invoked with POST. Operations can be bound to an entity or collection or be unbound. V2 exposes operation patterns through function imports.

Example
Get a calculated preview through a function when the supported service contract fits. Submit a request with an action that checks the business transition.

Avoid
An HTTP GET should not create or approve business documents.

column1: ODATA-06 | How do ETags prevent lost updates?
column2:
Short answer
A service returns a version token. The client supplies If-Match with a modifying request, and the service checks whether the current version matches. A stale token normally produces HTTP 412. The client should reload or resolve the conflict instead of silently overwriting newer changes.

Example
Test with two clients reading the same version, then updating sequentially. In RAP, configure the relevant ETag fields and update semantics correctly.

Avoid
If-Match with a wildcard can defeat the intended stale-version protection; timestamps alone do not secure authorization.
Two editors and one version: an illustrated story

Alice and Ben read version 7. Alice updates successfully, producing version 8. Ben must not overwrite that newer state using the stale version 7 precondition.
Explain it: Why should the client refresh and resolve the conflict instead of blindly retrying its old payload?
Limit: Version numbers are illustrative. Real ETags are opaque validators; a failed If-Match precondition commonly returns HTTP 412. This is optimistic concurrency, not a pessimistic lock.

column1: ODATA-07 | Is a batch request one database transaction?
column2:
Short answer
Not necessarily. A batch groups HTTP operations; it is not automatically one atomic transaction. Multipart batch formats use changesets for atomic change operations. OData 4.01 JSON batch uses atomicity groups. These mechanisms depend on protocol version and provider support; read operations and separate groups can have different outcomes. Deep create describes creating a related structure and requires backend support for a coherent transaction.

Example
For an order and items, test a failing child and verify that the intended atomic group does not partially persist. Inspect each inner response even when the outer batch request succeeds. Check the service's protocol version and provider capabilities; a V4 endpoint does not automatically support every V4.01 batching feature.

Avoid
HTTP 200 for a batch does not mean every operation inside it succeeded.

The outer envelope reduces HTTP packaging overhead; it does not establish one universal database transaction.

column1: ODATA-08 | What are MPC_EXT and DPC_EXT in classic Gateway?
column2:
Short answer
The model-provider extension class extends the service model and metadata. The data-provider extension class implements or redefines runtime data operations and business error handling. Generated base classes should not host customer changes. This is a classic Gateway development approach, distinct from RAP behavior implementation.

Example
In a SEGW service, trace GET_ENTITYSET for collection retrieval and CREATE_ENTITY or a deep-create implementation for writes. Keep reusable domain logic outside the provider adapter where feasible.

Avoid
Putting every rule directly in DPC_EXT makes testing and reuse harder; MPC_EXT is not intrinsically unimportant.

column1: ODATA-09 | How do authentication authorization and CSRF differ?
column2:
Short answer
Authentication establishes the caller. Authorization controls what that caller may access or change. CSRF protection mitigates unwanted requests using a user's browser session. SAP Gateway write flows commonly require a fetched CSRF token and matching session context; exact requirements depend on the endpoint and authentication flow.

Example
For a 403, inspect whether the failure is a missing token, service permission or business authorization. Never fix it by indiscriminately removing checks.

Avoid
CSRF is not a universal OData-standard requirement and a valid token does not grant business permission.

column1: ODATA-10 | How do you design dates media and errors?
column2:
Short answer
Preserve the service's protocol-specific date and timestamp types and timezone meaning. Media streams require the appropriate binary endpoints, content type and content handling. Errors need suitable HTTP status, stable codes and useful messages without exposing internals. Classic Gateway and RAP use different implementation contracts.

Example
Use a date for a date-only business value and a timezone-aware instant for a recorded event. In Gateway use its exception and message-container APIs; in RAP use FAILED and REPORTED appropriately.

Avoid

column1: ODATA-11 | How do you troubleshoot a slow or failing Fiori request?
column2:
Short answer
Capture the failing network request and response, user, timestamp and correlation information. Check service metadata and relevant Gateway or application logs, then trace SQL and ABAP work in an authorized test context. Separate UI rendering, network payload, backend processing and authorization failures.

A huge $expand can dominate response time even if each SQL statement is fast. Measure request duration, row counts and payload size before changing the model.

column1: ODATA-12 | How do you evolve an existing API safely?
column2:
Short answer
Treat keys, names, types, operation semantics and error behavior as consumer contracts. Prefer compatible additions where consumers tolerate them, and version breaking changes. Test old consumers and publish a transition plan. A parallel RAP service may coexist with a legacy Gateway service during modernization.

Renaming a field or changing a key can break saved UI state and integrations. Inventory consumers and retire the old contract only after migration evidence.

column2:

column2:
Short answer

column2:
Short answer
I first identify the supported business interface and deployment constraints. Standard APIs, IDocs, or migration tooling can preserve application validation and provide documented contracts. In classic environments BDC can be a fallback for a suitable screen-based process, but it is sensitive to screen flow and configuration. Volume, completeness, error recovery, and supportability drive the choice.

For a one-time migration, supported migration objects may be preferable to building a permanent integration. BDC is not a general option for ABAP Cloud. A BAPI's existence does not prove that it is released for the target development model or supports every needed field.

column1: RICEFW-03 | How do BAdIs, customer exits, and user exits differ?
column2:
Short answer
A BAdI exposes an object-oriented extension contract, with capabilities such as filters or multiple implementations depending on its definition. Classic customer exits include function, screen, and menu exits managed through enhancement projects. User exit often refers to older application-specific routines. I inspect the actual extension, its timing, and its supported release status before choosing it.

column1: RICEFW-04 | What is the difference between implicit and explicit enhancement options?
column2:
Short answer
Explicit enhancement options are deliberately provided in source, such as enhancement points or sections. Implicit options exist at predefined positions without an explicit marker there. A point adds implementation code, while a section can replace a defined section's implementation. Both are enhancement mechanisms; explicit enhancement does not automatically mean directly modifying SAP's original source.

Example
An enhancement spot organizes explicit options, while an enhancement implementation supplies customer code. A section replacement deserves particular care because it can bypass standard behavior. Availability and suitability differ from the released extension contracts expected in ABAP Cloud.

Avoid
The distinction is not 'implicit preserves SAP code, explicit modifies it'; source modification is a separate concept.

column1: RICEFW-05 | How would you design a reliable interface?
column2:
Short answer
I define the business contract, authentication, validation, mapping, response semantics, and operational recovery. Synchronous interfaces suit immediate results; asynchronous processing can decouple systems and tolerate temporary outages. I make duplicate handling, correlation identifiers, timeouts, retries, and reconciliation explicit. Choosing OData, SOAP, IDoc, or another supported API follows those requirements and the landscape.

Example
A network timeout after posting creates an uncertain outcome: blindly retrying may post twice. A business idempotency key and a way to query the original outcome help. Retry policies should distinguish transient technical failures from permanent validation errors.

Avoid
Transport-level success or an accepted message does not prove that the target business transaction was posted successfully.

The remote commit belongs to another system, so local failure needs an explicit recovery strategy.

column1: RICEFW-06 | How would you troubleshoot a failed IDoc in a classic system?
column2:
Short answer
I correlate the business document with the IDoc, inspect its control record, data, status history, and detailed messages, then identify configuration, mapping, master-data, authorization, or application errors. I resolve the cause before controlled reprocessing. I also determine whether the business effect already occurred and how duplicates are prevented before repeating a posting.

Example
WE02 or WE05 can support inspection, and BD87 can support reprocessing where authorized and appropriate. Partner profiles, ports, process codes, and application logs may explain the failure. The exact processing path depends on direction and configured integration.

Avoid
Changing a status or repeatedly reprocessing without checking business effects can hide the cause or create duplicates.

Follow the message to the business outcome. The AIF band represents supported configured capabilities, not an obligatory stage for every IDoc.

column1: RICEFW-07 | What makes a data conversion safe and supportable?
column2:
Short answer
I separate extraction, cleansing, mapping, validation, loading, and reconciliation. A conversion needs stable source identifiers, restart behavior, error records, and business totals that can be checked. Trial loads establish throughput and uncover data-quality issues. Cutover includes sequencing, freeze assumptions, ownership, and recovery plans, using supported business interfaces rather than uncontrolled table updates.

Example
For document migration, reconcile counts and values by company and currency, not only a total row count. Distinguish rejected records from accepted records whose follow-up processing is pending. Repeating a failed package must not recreate already posted documents.

Avoid
A technically successful load is not evidence that balances, relationships, and business status are correct.

column2:
Short answer

Adobe-based output forms are common in newer scenarios and require the appropriate rendering setup. S/4HANA output management coexists with other frameworks; I do not assume a universal BRF+ migration for every application.

Example
Separate output determination from form layout and data provision. Test language, fonts, multi-page item tables, totals, attachments, recipients, and reprints. An invoice rendering correctly once does not verify email routing, spool behavior, or all business variants.

All S/4HANA output is not automatically BRF+ plus Adobe, and an output form need not be an interactive form.

column1: RICEFW-09 | How do classic Workflow, Flexible Workflow, and SAP Build Process Automation differ?
column2:

SAP Build Process Automation runs on BTP and supports broader automation and integration. I choose according to the delivered scenario, landscape, extensibility, and operational needs.

For a supported purchase approval scenario, first evaluate the delivered Flexible Workflow features. For a cross-system custom process, a BTP option may fit. A custom RAP application does not automatically receive a complete approval workflow merely because it has a submit action.

column1: RICEFW-10 | What are a workflow container, task, work item, and agent?
column2:
Short answer
The container holds process context, and bindings map data between workflow components. A task defines work to perform; a work item is a runtime instance. Agent determination identifies the responsible processor, considering the scenario's rules and restrictions. A complete process also needs decisions, deadlines, exception handling, and a reliable update to the business object.

Example
For an approval, the context might carry a request identifier and amount rather than a stale copy of every field. If no valid approver is found, the design needs an explicit error or fallback path; silent continuation would violate the approval requirement.

column1: HTTP-03 | How do GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE differ?
column2:
Short answer

column1: HTTP-04 | What do safe and idempotent mean, and how do they affect retries?
column2:
Short answer

After a timeout on CreateOrder, the client may not know whether the server committed. Use a documented idempotency mechanism or query a stable business correlation before retrying. Repeated DELETE can return different statuses while the final resource state remains absent.

column1: HTTP-05 | Which HTTP statuses should an ABAP API developer explain?
column2:

column1: RFC-01 | How does a function module differ from an ABAP method?
column2:
Short answer
A function module is a callable procedure belonging to a function group, with a defined interface and potentially shared function-group state. A method belongs to a class or interface and supports object-oriented contracts and dependency substitution. I usually organize new business logic in classes while preserving function modules required by existing APIs, RFC, or framework integration.

A normal function module is not automatically remote-enabled or an update module; those are distinct attributes and invocation models. A thin, approved integration entry point can delegate calculations to a testable class without changing its external contract.

column1: RFC-02 | How do synchronous, asynchronous, transactional, queued, and background RFC differ?
column2:
Short answer
Synchronous RFC waits for the response. Asynchronous RFC lets the caller continue and optionally collect results through callbacks. Transactional RFC registers calls and parameters in the current SAP LUW; COMMIT WORK triggers processing of the registered unit rather than each call running immediately. Queued RFC adds sequencing through configured queues. Background RFC supports transactional and queued units with its own infrastructure. Their documented delivery guarantees apply to those units, not automatically to an entire distributed business process.

Example
A tRFC registration does not prove completed remote processing. ROLLBACK WORK removes the current registrations; after commit, temporary unavailability is handled through retry. sRFC and aRFC lack that durable retry model. tRFC and bgRFC type T provide documented Exactly Once unit semantics; qRFC and bgRFC type Q add ordering within the configured dependency scope. bgRFC is the successor technology; choose what the target environment permits and let the runtime own the unit's transaction. Separate business submissions can still duplicate an order.

Avoid
STARTING NEW TASK is not durable background messaging, and queued processing does not imply one global order across unrelated queues.

column1: RFC-03 | What is the difference between a BAPI and an RFC-enabled function module?
column2:

A released classic BAPI may be suitable for an existing integration while not being released for direct ABAP Cloud use. Conversely, modern released business APIs can use HTTP and OData instead of a classic BAPI implementation. The name alone does not establish clean-core classification.

column2:
Short answer

A successful transport response is not enough: inspect all relevant business return messages and the commit result. Some documented legacy BAPIs commit internally. In RAP behavior implementations, inserting BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT is not a valid way to bypass framework transaction restrictions.

The callback can correlate the task identifier with its input package, then store a result or failure. The caller must remain alive and allow callback processing, using an appropriate bounded wait when needed. Callback order need not match the launch order.

Common inbound statuses include 51 for an application posting error, 53 for an application document posted, and 64 for readiness to transfer to the application. Outbound status 03 means data was passed to the port; it does not prove successful business posting in the receiver.

Example
Outbound 30 commonly means ready for dispatch. An inbound 53 is still evidence about that configured processing step, not every downstream business process. Check linked document references and scenario-specific acknowledgments when the requirement is end-to-end confirmation.

Avoid
Do not treat every low-numbered status as failure or map an outbound success code directly to an inbound business success guarantee.

column1: INTF-05 | How would you investigate an IDoc that is missing or has failed?
column2:
Short answer
I start with sender, receiver, message type, business key, and time, then locate the IDoc and inspect its control data, segments, and status history. I separate generation, routing, transport, syntax, and application failures. Classic tools such as WE02 or WE05 support inspection; communication and application monitors explain failures beyond the IDoc record itself.

Example
If the sender shows dispatch but the receiver has no IDoc, investigate the technical channel and relevant RFC or middleware queue. If the receiver has status 51, inspect the application error, master data, mapping, and authorizations before changing connectivity settings.

column1: INTF-06 | How do you reprocess an IDoc without creating duplicate business documents?
column2:
Short answer
I identify and correct the root cause, confirm whether any business effect already occurred, and choose the supported reprocessing path for that status and scenario. I preserve correlation and audit history and verify the result after retry. Duplicate prevention should use a stable business identity or application contract, not only an assumption about the technical message number.

Example
BD87 supports classic status-based reprocessing where appropriate. Recreating a message or using a test copy can produce a new technical identity and bypass duplicate protection tied only to the original one. A partial or uncertain outcome needs reconciliation before another posting attempt.

Avoid
Changing a status to look successful, or creating another IDoc blindly, does not repair the original error and may duplicate its business effect.

column1: INTF-07 | What is SAP Application Interface Framework, and what is it not?
column2:
Short answer
AIF provides configurable interface processing, monitoring, and error-handling capabilities so technical and business users can investigate messages in a meaningful context. Depending on the scenario, it can organize mappings, checks, actions, and recovery. It does not replace the underlying transport or automatically monitor every interface. Availability, delivered content, and custom-development usage rights must be verified.

Example
SAP distinguishes full custom-interface use from limited runtime rights supplied with particular products. Seeing an AIF monitor in a system does not establish permission to build arbitrary custom AIF interfaces. Confirm the target product's current scope and the customer's entitlement before proposing that implementation.

Avoid
AIF is not a substitute for RFC, IDoc, OData, or middleware, and its presence does not establish unrestricted licensing or identical cloud capabilities.

column1: INTF-08 | How do AIF structure mappings, value mappings, checks, and actions work together?
column2:
Short answer
Structure mapping transforms the message shape, while value mapping translates business codes between representations. Checks validate applicable conditions, and actions perform configured processing such as calling application logic. I separate these responsibilities, version their contracts, and preserve useful error context. The actual execution sequence and underlying engine depend on the configured interface.

Example
An external company code may map to an internal company code, then be checked before an application posting action. A missing mapping should identify the source value and responsible owner. An action must respect the application's commit, authorization, and duplicate-handling rules.

Avoid
Passing AIF checks does not replace the target application's business validation, and arbitrary commits inside processing actions can break coordinated recovery.

column1: INTF-09 | How would you configure useful and secure AIF monitoring?
column2:
Short answer
I expose meaningful business keys for searching, assign responsibility and alerts to the correct recipients, and provide enough context to distinguish mapping, validation, and technical failures. Authorization must separate viewing, editing, restarting, and canceling messages. In classic AIF, controls can be scoped by namespace, interface, version, and activity; applicable field restrictions must also be considered.

Example
A business operator may need to inspect a failed cost-center mapping but should not automatically receive access to every payload or permission to edit amounts. Transactions such as /AIF/IFMON and /AIF/ERR are relevant where installed; cloud monitoring uses its supported apps and roles.

Avoid
Recipient assignment or visibility in a monitor is not a replacement for authorization, and broad payload access can expose sensitive business information.

column1: INTF-10 | What must you establish before resubmitting or editing a message in AIF?
column2:
Short answer
I establish which engine owns the message, what processing already succeeded, which fields may be corrected, and what the configured restart operation actually repeats. After correcting the cause, an authorized resubmission must follow that ownership and preserve the audit trail. I do not assume every AIF interface persists or restarts data in exactly the same way.

Example
An interface using underlying IDoc processing and an interface using AIF-controlled actions can have different restart behavior. Avoid concurrent retries from both the underlying technical monitor and AIF. Verify the target document and message status after a retry, especially following a timeout.

Avoid
AIF resubmission does not roll back an earlier committed document and is not automatically equivalent to creating a new business request.

column1: INTF-11 | When would you use OData, IDoc, or AIF?
column2:
Short answer
OData is an HTTP-based service protocol useful for supported queries and business operations, including UI and system integration. IDoc provides structured messages and established asynchronous application integration scenarios. AIF adds processing and operational capabilities around supported interfaces. They address different concerns and can coexist; I choose the business contract and delivery model before selecting monitoring.

Example
A UI reading current request status may use OData while an established partner sends order messages as IDocs. AIF can support operational error handling where the integration is configured for it. Replacing one technology solely because another is newer ignores available contracts and recovery needs.

Avoid
AIF is not a third wire protocol, OData is not limited to UI use, and IDoc is not restricted to batch-only dispatch.

column1: INTF-12 | What security and end-to-end tests would you require for an IDoc or AIF interface?
column2:
Short answer

Reconciliation must compare business counts and values, not only green monitor statuses.

column1: SQLX-01 | A CDS table function joins client-dependent purchasing data in SQLScript, writes a helper table, and assumes the outer CDS DCL protects every internal read. Would you approve it?
column2:
Short answer
No. For the documented CDS table-function contract, the AMDP database function is read-only, uses SQLScript on HANA and must satisfy the applicable client-safety rules. I would remove the write and review every source, join and client boundary rather than trust an outer annotation. Client isolation and business authorization are separate concerns: establish protection at the supported consumption path and do not assume SQLScript reproduces ABAP SQL or CDS access-control behavior automatically. Confirm target-release and language-version eligibility first.

Example
Use two clients containing the same business key and two users with different purchasing scopes. Verify that results, aggregates and error behavior cannot expose foreign data. Check the declared return types and result grain as well as the USING dependencies. Prefer a supported CDS or ABAP SQL expression if it already meets the requirement; a table function adds a database-specific contract.

Avoid
Treating every AMDP method as read-only, or treating this read-only table-function constraint as permission to read any SAP table. General AMDP capabilities and eligible dependencies are separate.
HANA pushdown: result grain and table-function review

A two-language text join duplicates both item amounts. Repair the relationship before accepting a performance rewrite, then verify security, client isolation and the chosen implementation contract.
Explain it: Why would DISTINCT or dividing by two be an unreliable repair, and what metrics would justify pushdown?
Limit: Illustrative data, not a benchmark. Read-only here refers to the cited CDS table-function scenario, not every AMDP method; check target rules and consumption-path security.

  • What evidence shows that both client isolation and the consumer's business authorization are enforced?

  • Reviews client safety and authorization as separate boundaries

column1: SQLX-02 | A report transfers one million item rows to ABAP to calculate totals. A rewrite uses AMDP but doubles amounts after a text join. Which implementation would you recommend?
column2:
Short answer
First establish the required result grain and repair the text relationship; a faster wrong aggregate is unacceptable. Then compare a supported ABAP SQL or CDS aggregation with AMDP only if its extra database capabilities are actually needed. Push selective filters and suitable aggregation toward the database to reduce transferred data, while preserving authorization, currencies, null handling and multiplicity. Measure database work, transferred rows and end-to-end time under representative volume rather than claiming SQLScript is inherently faster.

Example
For order 4711, two items worth 40 and 60 EUR should total 100 EUR. Joining each item to two language texts produces four rows and a wrong 200 EUR total. Restrict the relationship or aggregate at the correct boundary as required by the semantics. Verify equivalent results before comparing traces; fewer returned rows alone does not prove less database work.

Avoid
Using DISTINCT or dividing by a current duplication factor without fixing the grain, or selecting AMDP simply because HANA is present.

A two-language text join duplicates both item amounts. Repair the relationship before accepting a performance rewrite, then verify security, client isolation and the chosen implementation contract.

column1: DELIV-01 | A pull request passes local linting and its ABAP sources are pushed with abapGit. The team calls the cloud feature deployed. What evidence and delivery steps are missing?
column2:
Short answer
Git records source history; abapGit transfers supported development objects. Neither statement proves target activation or productive delivery. Establish the product-specific lifecycle route, software component and dependency order; BTP ABAP environment can use supported transport/gCTS or add-on delivery scenarios, while other ABAP Cloud environments have their own routes. Tie the source revision to target syntax/activation, ATC, meaningful ABAP Unit and integration results, then verify the imported revision, service access and configuration in the intended system.

Example
A CI result must name what actually ran and where: local lint is not SAP activation, and mocked tests do not prove runtime authorization. Include dependency versions, transport or delivery identifiers, import evidence, communication setup and recovery ownership. Keep technical identities and secrets out of Git. A source export can support review without representing a complete deployable application.

Avoid
Equating an abapGit push with a transport release, treating gCTS and abapGit as interchangeable names, or applying one BTP delivery route to every ABAP Cloud product.
Source transfer, delivery and verified runtime evidence

Four evidence layers answer different questions. A release links the reviewed and tested revision to an actual imported state, then verifies the target consumer and configuration.
Explain it: Which artifact proves what was imported, and what can fail after a successful import?
Limit: REV-42, D-17 and TST are fictional identifiers. The table is an evidence checklist, not a mandatory sequence requiring abapGit in every transport landscape.

Interviewer follow-ups
  • How would you prove the tested source revision is the one imported into the target?
  • Which prerequisites can make an active service fail after an otherwise successful import?
Strong answer criteria
  • Separates source control, source transfer and runtime delivery
  • Chooses a lifecycle route for the actual product
  • Requires traceable target checks and operational readiness
Verification evidence
Record commit, component/dependency versions and delivery IDs; retain target activation/ATC/test/import logs and a service smoke test with an authorized and a denied identity.
